title: Federal laboratory-equipment disposal can expose export-control and biosecurity gaps while malicious use remains unobserved
source_unit: U.S. Government Accountability Office GAO-26-107729 review of public-health and national-security risks in disposal of federal laboratory equipment
geography: United States federal laboratory equipment disposed of by HHS and USDA through GSA transfer, sale, and auction processes

observations.period: Fiscal years 2022–2025 equipment sales and September 1, 2026 GAO report publicly released October 1

denominator.unit: pieces of unneeded HHS and USDA laboratory equipment sold during fiscal years 2022–2025

controlled_items_sold.unit: freeze dryers and mass spectrometers identified by GAO as on the Commerce Control List and sold to U.S. and Canadian individuals or companies, some appearing to be resellers

control_reporting_failure.value: HHS and USDA did not report the nine Commerce Control List items to GSA as required by federal regulations

acquisition_test.unit: pieces of HHS and USDA laboratory equipment successfully acquired by GAO using fictitious identities, including a nonprofit organization, that experts said could pose a biosecurity risk

risk_assessment.value: HHS and USDA had not assessed biosecurity risks associated with disposal, including acquisition by actors seeking to create biological weapons or obtain sensitive information

system_design_gap.value: HHS policy was silent on the reporting requirement and GSA's property-management system lacked a standard approach, such as a dedicated field, to identify Commerce Control List equipment

open_recommendations.unit: open recommendations to GSA, HHS, and USDA on control-list identification and biosecurity risk assessment and mitigation

malicious_conversion.unit: recipient intent, export, biological-weapon development, sensitive-information recovery, harm, or completed mitigation

observations.method: Structured extraction from GAO-26-107729, based on GSA disposal data for fiscal years 2022–2025, federal regulations, a fictitious-identity acquisition test, interviews with agency officials, and a visit to a decommissioned federal laboratory. Disposal scale, controlled items, reporting failure, acquisition test, risk assessment, control design, recommendations, and malicious outcomes are retained as separate stages.
observations.uncertainty: The four acquired pieces were a designed test and do not estimate the probability of malicious use. The nine controlled items are a reviewed subset of 1,316 sales, and identifying an equipment type as biosecurity-relevant does not establish recipient intent, export, weapon development, data recovery, or harm. Decontamination and other disposal controls may reduce some risks not captured by the public summary.
observations.subgroup: Federal agencies, laboratory workers, equipment recipients and resellers, public-health and national-security institutions, and communities exposed to consequences of laboratory-equipment misuse.
observations.counterinterpretation: Equipment resale can conserve public resources and equipment may be decontaminated or repurposed safely; export controls and GSA processes may address risks through other channels, while a dedicated reporting field and recurring risk assessment could improve visibility without proving that prior sales caused harm.

related_sources.claim: The official accessible report contains the disposal cohort, controlled-item, acquisition-test, risk-assessment, and recommendation findings.
The official report PDF provides the complete public-health and national-security disposal review.

boundary: This record advances a bounded federal laboratory-equipment disposal-to-export-control and biosecurity-risk route. It does not establish recipient intent, export, biological-weapon development, sensitive-information recovery, public harm, or completed mitigation.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Canonical GAO product URL string used as a stable source identifier; accessible report and PDF links are retained for reproduction.
